body.text: Few places or corridors tell a richer story of geography and human movement than Béjaïa. Stepping into its history reveals how trade, terrain, and culture shaped the modern map.

Béjaïa (Kabyle: ⴱⴳⴰⵢⴻⵜ, romanized: Bgayet, Arabic: بجاية), also formerly known as Bougie in French, is a Mediterranean port city and commune on the Gulf of Béjaïa in Algeria, it is the capital of Béjaïa Province, 220 kilometers east of Algiers.

The site of the city has been inhabited since the Paleolithic era. Neolithic remains found in the region belong to the Iberomaurusian culture. The city was first mentioned in historical sources dating back to the 5th century BC as part of the Libyan-Berber world.

Open to maritime trade, the city experienced Phoenician influence and established a trading post, which led to it being known as Salda, and in Roman times, as Saldae. The Vandals would settle there before abandoning the city and transferring their capital to Carthage.

The city was Islamized from the 8th century onwards, being captured by the Arabs in 708 and then mentioned again in the 10th century by Andalusian geographer Abu Ubayd al-Bakri, who spoke of a significant Andalusian presence.

It became a prestigious capital as well as a religious, commercial, and scholarly center of the Mediterranean under the Hammadid dynasty in the 11th century, who integrated it as their capital in place of Qal'at Bani Hammad.

After an Almohad occupation, it once again became the capital of a branch of the Hafsids and then the seat of an independent sultanate. Renowned in Europe for the quality of its beeswax candles, Bejaia also played a significant role in the dissemination of Arabic numerals and local mathematical knowledge to the west.

In the Middle Ages, scholars such as Raymond Lull, Leonardo Fibonacci, and Ibn Khaldun studied there. After a gradual decline that started in the 15th century, Bejaia was conquered by the Spanish in 1510, suffering a further decline that continued after its reconquest by the Regency of Algiers in 1555.

It substantially lost its scholarly culture, its major educational institutions disappeared and its leading scientists had moved to other major cities in the Maghreb and Near East. Only decentralized theological institutions of the zawiyas remained. It was eclipsed, on the scale of the central Maghreb, by Algiers, the seat of political power and the navy.
It continued to attract some prestige from its religious mystics and the export of timber from its hinterland.

It was taken by the French in 1833. It then continued its decline to become only an average port city, exporting local agricultural products, before regaining some dynamism at the end of the 19th century.

During the Algerian War, the region contributed a significant territory within the historic Wilaya III, which encompassed a large part of Kabylia. It played a vital role in the political, military, and logistical networks of the National Liberation Front and the National Liberation Army. Activists contributed to structuring networks and coordinating revolutionary activities.
Upon the country's independence in 1962, it regained its cultural role. It also gradually regained its status as a major port, rivaling other major Algerian cities.
With 177,888 people according to the 2008 census, Bejaia is the largest city in Kabylia and is the cultural capital of Lesser Kabylia.

Thanks to its geographical location, it is also the most important industrial center in the region, notably due to the concentration of numerous industries and the presence of one of the largest oil and commercial ports in the Mediterranean. It also has an international airport.
Geography
Location

Béjaïa owes its existence to its port, which also makes it prosperous. It is located in a sickle-shaped bay protected from the swell of offshore winds (northwest facing) by the advance of Cape Carbon (to the west of the city). The city is backed by Mount Gouraya located in a northwest position.

This port site, in one of the most beautiful bays of the Maghreb and Mediterranean coast, is dominated in the background by the Babors mountain range. Another advantage is that the city is the outlet of the Soummam valley, a geographical corridor facing southwest.
However, since the time when the city was a capital, there has been a divorce between the city and the region (Kabylia) linked to the difficulty of securing a hinterland.
On a macro-regional scale, the city has its back to the region: its position at the end of the Soummam places it at the interface between Grande and Petite Kabylie. ) by turning away from the coast.

The city has, in a way, weak local roots, the rural proximity of the city is limited to four or five communes. On a micro-regional scale, Béjaïa is the outlet of a central Algeria, going from Algiers to Skikda, the spillway of the Highlands and a supply port for two million people.

But the connection is complex: to the south-east, trade with Sétif is only possible through the steep gorges of Kherrata, another route takes the Soummam, then to the east the Iron Gates and the climb towards Bordj Bou Arreridj, it is this route that is taken by the national road and the railway.
These topographical constraints mean that, despite its strong dynamism, the city sees part of the trade escape it in its eastern and western areas of influence.

The town is overlooked by the mountain Yemma Gouraya. Other nearby scenic spots include the Aiguades beach and the Pic des Singes (Peak of the Monkeys), the latter site is a habitat for the endangered Barbary macaque, which prehistorically had a much broader distribution than at present.
All three of these geographic features are located in the Gouraya National Park.

The urban area covers an area of 12,022 hectares. 5 km northeast of Bordj Bou Arreridj, 70 km northwest of Sétif and 61 km west of Jijel. The geographic coordinates of the commune at the central point of its capital are 36° 45′ 00″ North and 5° 04′ 00″ East, respectively.
Toponymy
Béjaïa is transliteration from an Arabic toponym derived from the Berber toponym (Kabyle variant) Bgayet, notably by transliteration (see Transcription and transliteration) of the sound ǧ in dj (ج).

This Berber name, which would have originally been Tabgayet, but whose initial t marking the feminine gender would have fallen into disuse, would come from the words tabegga, tabeɣayt, meaning "wild brambles and blackberries". In Tifinagh script, the name of the city is ⴱⴳⴰⵢⴻⵜ (Bgayet).
The name Béjaïa would thus originally have the same Berber root as other names of cities in the Maghreb, such as Dougga (Thouga) and Béja (Vaga) in Tunisia or Ksar Baghaï (Bagaï) in the Aurès.

In medieval Romance languages, Bugaya (from Arabic Bugāya, in Spanish Bujía and in Italian Bugía is the name given to the city, which supplied a large quantity of beeswax for the manufacture of candles. Bougie became the French form of this transcription of the Arabic name.
Gradually it came to refer to the wax that was imported in the Middle Ages for the manufacture of candles in Europe, they are from then on commonly designated in French by the word "bougie".
This in turn is carried over to the word Bugia, meaning a long-handled candlestick used by Catholic bishops and high-ranking priests.
Climate and hydrography
The city is part of the Soummam's drainage basin. Béjaïa and the lower Soummam Valley enjoy a Mediterranean climate. It is generally humid with a slight seasonal temperature change.

In addition to the Soummam River, which sufficiently meets agricultural needs in the surroundings of the city, Béjaïa is located in the maritime Kabylie and benefits from a fairly favorable rainfall compared to the rest of the country.
The rainfall in the region can range from 800 mm to 1,200 mm, but some local sources tend to be depleted due to increased demand.

The city also draws its water resources from the mountainous hinterland and from various springs, such as that of Toudja, which was connected in ancient times by an aqueduct to the ancient city (Saldae).
Roadside and rail communications

The city of Béjaïa is linked to Algiers, Tizi Ouzou, Bouira, Sétif, Jijel and several Kabyle localities by an important road network. It has a bus station. Bus lines connect it to the cities of the Algerian south, including Hassi Messaoud, Ouargla, Ghardaïa, Laghouat, Djelfa and Bou Saâda.
